performers: San Francisco Symphony Orchestra, Pierre Monteux; Naoum Blinder, violin
question: How much can orchestration change while a melody remains recognisable?
intro: A bassoon melody follows the violin’s framing solo, then passes through changing instrumental colours and sharper orchestral episodes. Listen for variation of a recognisable contour rather than a new character at every solo.

cues.text: The score gives the first principal-theme statement to bassoon over a quiet string foundation. Its nasal lower-register colour differs sharply from the introductory violin.

cues.text: The principal melody passes to the oboe in the early variations. Compare its clearer attack with the bassoon’s preceding statement while retaining the same melodic outline in memory.

cues.title: Variation through orchestration
cues.text: The movement develops its melody by changing scoring, accompaniment and rhythmic activity. A variation can preserve the recognisable tune while altering how the surrounding texture moves.

cues.title: Teaching before complete confidence
cues.text: Rimsky-Korsakov became a professor at the Saint Petersburg Conservatory in 1871. His later autobiography describes how the appointment pushed him to strengthen his own technique while teaching others.
cues.evidence: Historical note, not a timed musical event. Rimsky-Korsakov, My Musical Life, translated by Judah A. Joffe, second edition, chapter X, pp. 100–103: the summer 1871 invitation and autumn appointment, his lack of technical preparation, and his account of becoming a pupil himself while teaching. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/72/IMSLP721391-PMLP52433-My_Musical_Life_eng_edt.pdf

cues.text: Sharper brass figures contrast with the longer wind melody. Listen for the difference between an announcing gesture and a phrase that continues over several bars.

cues.text: The score places a clarinet solo above tremolo strings in the central span. Repeated bow strokes provide a moving background without competing with the wind line’s contour.

cues.text: The principal melody remains a point of reference through the movement’s changing episodes. Recognition depends on its contour and rhythm even when its orchestral setting grows heavier.

cues.text: When orchestral reinforcement is removed, follow what remains of the melodic line. The withdrawal can expose the relationship between a wind phrase and its string support.

cues.title: A later explanation of the headings
cues.text: In My Musical Life, Rimsky-Korsakov explains that the descriptive titles were intended only as slight guidance. His account encourages attention to recurring musical material rather than a fixed catalogue of depicted events.
cues.evidence: Historical or source-context note; no timed musical event is asserted. https://www.laphil.com/works/scheherazade

cues.title: The bassoon colour returns
cues.text: The score recovers the bassoon’s characteristic sound in the later principal-theme return. Compare its line with the opening statement instead of expecting a new character whenever the solo register changes.
cues.evidence: General listening point about the written movement, not an instrument entrance or bar-aligned claim at this timestamp. https://www.laphil.com/works/scheherazade Score: https://archive.org/download/Cantorion_sheet_music_collection_5/6217645a277f7b147a1088840c0845b4.pdf

cues.title: A major-mode final chord
cues.text: The movement begins from B minor but closes in B major. The major third changes the final sonority without undoing the minor-key material that has dominated the movement.

transitions.title: Violin yields to bassoon
transitions.how: The violin-and-harp frame gives way to the bassoon’s principal melody over a quiet string foundation. The register and timbre change sharply, while the new phrase establishes the material for subsequent variation.
transitions.evidence: Approximate passage boundary, not a bar alignment. cache/analysis/rimsky-korsakov-scheherazade-kalendar.txt: The 0:34 boundary accompanies a large drop in spectral brightness, from roughly 2800 Hz at 0:30 to 810 Hz at 0:35; the score identifies bassoon, not that measurement alone. Written design: https://www.laphil.com/works/scheherazade Score: https://archive.org/download/Cantorion_sheet_music_collection_5/6217645a277f7b147a1088840c0845b4.pdf

transitions.title: A melodic account is interrupted
transitions.how: The varied principal melody leads into sharper brass gestures. Short announcing figures and changed orchestral emphasis interrupt the longer wind-led phrases rather than simply repeating them more loudly.
transitions.evidence: Approximate passage boundary, not a bar alignment. cache/analysis/rimsky-korsakov-scheherazade-kalendar.txt: A strong boundary at 2:58 follows a quieter 2:55 window; abrupt level changes continue through 3:05–3:35. Written design: https://www.laphil.com/works/scheherazade Score: https://archive.org/download/Cantorion_sheet_music_collection_5/6217645a277f7b147a1088840c0845b4.pdf

transitions.title: The ensemble leaves a solo exposed
transitions.how: The preceding orchestral crest recedes to a more exposed woodwind episode. Clarinet above tremolo strings creates motion in the background while leaving the melodic line distinct.
transitions.evidence: Approximate passage boundary, not a bar alignment. cache/analysis/rimsky-korsakov-scheherazade-kalendar.txt: The 3:55 crest gives way to a large reduction at 4:05; the score’s solo-and-tremolo region is placed broadly, not as an exact clarinet entrance. Written design: https://www.laphil.com/works/scheherazade Score: https://archive.org/download/Cantorion_sheet_music_collection_5/6217645a277f7b147a1088840c0845b4.pdf

transitions.title: The accompaniment becomes active
transitions.how: The exposed episode gives way to more active exchanges and fuller scoring. Moving accompaniment, repeated figures and changing instrumental groups carry familiar material through a larger central span.
transitions.evidence: Approximate passage boundary, not a bar alignment. cache/analysis/rimsky-korsakov-scheherazade-kalendar.txt: The 4:36 boundary precedes rising level and brightness across 4:35–5:15, followed by further strong passages. Written design: https://www.laphil.com/works/scheherazade Score: https://archive.org/download/Cantorion_sheet_music_collection_5/6217645a277f7b147a1088840c0845b4.pdf

transitions.title: A lower-register statement returns
transitions.how: After the central orchestral expansion, the principal material returns in a different harmonic and instrumental setting. A reduced lower-register foreground makes the recollection distinct from the preceding fuller scoring.
transitions.evidence: Approximate passage boundary, not a bar alignment. cache/analysis/rimsky-korsakov-scheherazade-kalendar.txt: The strong 6:26 boundary coincides with a large drop in level and brightness after the 6:20 crest; the new region remains reduced through roughly 7:05. Written design: https://www.laphil.com/works/scheherazade Score: https://archive.org/download/Cantorion_sheet_music_collection_5/6217645a277f7b147a1088840c0845b4.pdf

transitions.title: The theme broadens again
transitions.how: The transformed return expands into a stronger orchestral statement. Increased doubling and reinforcement enlarge the same melodic argument without requiring a new principal theme.
transitions.evidence: Approximate passage boundary, not a bar alignment. cache/analysis/rimsky-korsakov-scheherazade-kalendar.txt: The 7:20 boundary marks a jump to about −6 dB and a sustained stronger span through 8:35. Written design: https://www.laphil.com/works/scheherazade Score: https://archive.org/download/Cantorion_sheet_music_collection_5/6217645a277f7b147a1088840c0845b4.pdf

transitions.title: The close begins by withdrawing
transitions.how: The broad return loses orchestral weight before the closing recollections and final build. Wind-led phrases and their quieter foundation prepare a B-major ending after the movement’s predominantly minor-key course.
transitions.evidence: Approximate passage boundary, not a bar alignment. cache/analysis/rimsky-korsakov-scheherazade-kalendar.txt: The strongest boundaries at 8:42 and 8:54 accompany the marked reduction; a later boundary at 9:32 precedes the final rise towards 10:10. source.title: Rimsky-Korsakov, Scheherazade, II, full-score scan
source.locator: PDF pp. 1–3 violin frame and bassoon/oboe theme; p. 8 brass episode; p. 9 clarinet/tremolo; p. 19 piccolo, triangle and cymbals; pp. 25–30 return and ending. Times are approximate passage anchors.

timeline.note: Opening frame: violin above harp chords.
Bassoon theme over a quiet string foundation, anchored broadly to the 0:34 change.
Early variation: oboe takes the melodic foreground, with bassoon, horn and string support (PDF p. 3).
The early variations expand into string-led and wind-coloured statements across the 1:44 region.
Sharper brass episode: announcing figures interrupt the preceding principal-theme variations (PDF p. 8); broad anchor at 2:58.
Exposed clarinet against string tremolo after the 4:05 reduction (PDF p. 9); no bar-exact solo entry claimed.
Active central expansion: piccolo, brass, timpani, triangle and cymbals reinforce the changing texture across this larger region (including PDF p. 19).
Reduced lower-register return after the 6:26 boundary, with bassoon-led phrases and string support.
Broader return: fuller winds, brass and percussion contribute across the sustained 7:20–8:35 span.
Closing recollection: lighter wind-led statements replace the fuller scoring after 8:42.
Final build: winds, brass and percussion reinforce the B-major close across 10:00–10:20; the last chord then decays.

composer.epithet: A naval officer turned teacher who made orchestral register and symmetrical scales the machinery of Russian fairy-tale opera.
facts: Naval College in Saint Petersburg; composition with Mily Balakirev, followed by intensive private study
Saint Petersburg Conservatory from 1871; inspector of naval bands, 1873–84
Married the pianist and composer Nadezhda Purgold in 1872; she assisted with arrangements and editorial work
Fifteen operas, three symphonies, orchestral suites and overtures, songs and teaching books
composer.background:
Rimsky-Korsakov was born in Tikhvin into a family with a tradition of naval service. He entered the Naval College in Saint Petersburg in 1856, while continuing piano lessons and attending opera. His teacher Fyodor Kanille introduced him to Balakirev in 1861. The young officer began a symphony before he had the theoretical equipment expected of a conservatory composition student. A naval voyage on the clipper Almaz took him abroad in 1862–65, interrupting regular contact with the circle while work on the symphony continued. Balakirev conducted the First Symphony in Saint Petersburg in 1865.

His early colleagues included Mussorgsky, Borodin and Cui. With Balakirev they became the group known as the Five, united by friendship and cultural argument despite their differing methods. Rimsky-Korsakov’s orchestral picture Sadko, first written in 1867, already connects a supernatural subject with an unusual pitch organisation. The sea musician’s underwater world encouraged scales and chord relationships outside ordinary major and minor. His experience of ships and oceans gave the subject a biographical setting.
